extracted.intended_audience: jury members (and judges/litigators) in U.S. patent infringement trials
extracted.subtask_description: Model jury instructions describing claim construction and the legal standards for determining patent infringement and invalidity, including literal infringement, joint infringement, means-/step-plus-function rules, doctrine of equivalents, inducement/contributory theories, and statutory theories under 35 U.S.C. §271. Intended to be read to jurors in a patent trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim Construction—Generally
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent claims are numbered sentences at the end of the patent. The claims are intended to define, in words, the boundaries of the inventor’s rights. Only the claims of the patent can be infringed. Neither the written description, nor the drawings of a patent can be infringed. Each of the claims must be considered individually. You must use the same claim meaning for both your decision on infringement and your decision on invalidity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before deciding infringement or invalidity, jurors must understand the patent claims; only the claims—read and interpreted—define what can be infringed. Citations: 35 U.S.C. § 112; Phillips v. AWH Corp.; Markman; Catalina Lighting; SmithKline Diagnostics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim Construction for the Case (judge-provided meanings)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the judge's job to provide to you the meaning of any claim language that must be interpreted. You must accept the meanings the judge gives you and use them when you decide whether any claim has been infringed and whether any claim is invalid. The meaning of the words of the patent claims must be the same when deciding both infringement and invalidity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For claim limitations the court has not construed, jurors are to use the plain and ordinary meaning as understood by a person of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the alleged invention. (Teva v. Sandoz; Phillips; Markman.) The judge will read stipulations and the court's claim constructions to the jury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of Means-/Step-Plus-Function Claims
rubrics_metrics.description: For limitations in means[[step]]-plus-function format, the element does not cover all means/steps that perform the recited function. The court determines the recited function and the corresponding structure/step described in the specification (or an equivalent of that structure/step).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The jury must use the court's interpretation of the means-plus-function/step-plus-function element when deliberating on infringement and validity. Citations: 35 U.S.C. § 112; Mettler-Toledo; JVW Enterprises; Utah Med. Prods.; Valmont Indus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement—Generally (claim-by-claim assessment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Infringement is assessed claim-by-claim. Patent law gives the owner of a valid patent the right to exclude others from importing, making, using, offering to sell, or selling the claimed invention in the United States during the patent term. Any person or entity that has engaged in those acts without permission infringes the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When deciding infringement, jurors must compare the accused product/method to the patent claims (not to the plaintiff's product/method). Distinguish direct vs indirect infringement; literal infringement vs doctrine of equivalents; induced vs contributory infringement for indirect theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct Infringement—Knowledge and Intent Immaterial
rubrics_metrics.description: A defendant is liable for direct infringement if the plaintiff proves by a preponderance of the evidence that the defendant made, used, imported, offered to sell, or sold the invention defined in at least one claim during the patent term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct infringement can occur without knowledge of the patent or intent to infringe. (35 U.S.C. § 271(a); Commil; Medtronic v. Mirowski; Global-Tech; Warner-Jenkinson.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct Infringement—Literal Infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent claim is literally infringed only if the defendant’s accused product/method includes each and every element/method step recited in that patent claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate literal infringement separately for each asserted claim. The same accused element may satisfy more than one claim element. If the accused product/method does not contain one or more elements of a claim, it does not literally infringe that claim. (Limelight; Hutchins; Gen. Mills; Amstar.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct Infringement—Joint Infringement (attribution to others)
rubrics_metrics.description: A defendant may directly infringe if (1) the defendant personally performed all acts necessary to infringe, or (2) the steps performed by another party are attributable to the defendant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steps are attributable if the defendant exercised direction or control over the other party when the acts were performed, or if the defendant and the other party formed a joint enterprise. A joint enterprise requires proof of (1) an agreement among members, (2) a common purpose, (3) a community of pecuniary interest, and (4) an equal right to a voice in direction. If neither personal performance nor attribution is shown, there is no direct infringement. (Limelight; Eli Lilly v. Teva; Akamai; Nalco.) Practice note: distinguish joint infringement from inducement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literal Infringement of Means-/Step-Plus-Function Claims
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish infringement of a means-/step-plus-function claim, the plaintiff must prove by a preponderance that (1) the accused part/step performs the recited function, and (2) is identical or equivalent to the structure/step described in the specification for performing that function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First decide whether the accused product/method has any structure/step that performs the specified function. If yes, decide whether that structure/step is the same as or equivalent to the structure/step recited in the specification from the perspective of a person of ordinary skill. Equivalence can be shown by insubstantial differences or by performing substantially the same function in substantially the same way to achieve substantially the same result. If function not performed or structure not same/equivalent, the means-plus-function claim is not infringed. (35 U.S.C. § 112; Williamson; Gen. Protecht; Applied Med. Res.; A1-Site.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement of Dependent Claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Independent claims do not refer to other claims. Dependent claims refer to at least one other claim and include all elements of the independent claim(s) they refer to in addition to the elements recited in the dependent claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To establish literal infringement of a dependent claim, the plaintiff must show the accused product/method includes each and every element of both the independent claim and the dependent claim. If the independent claim is not literally infringed, the dependent claim cannot be literally infringed. (35 U.S.C. § 112; Jeneric/Pentron; Wahpeton Canvas; Shatterproof Glass.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim Preamble/Transitional Phrases—"Comprising", "Consisting of", "Consisting essentially of"
rubrics_metrics.description: "Comprising" means including the following but not excluding others. "Consisting of" means including the following and excluding others. "Consisting essentially of" means including the following and possibly including unlisted components/steps that do not materially affect the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim uses "comprising," additional components/steps do not preclude literal infringement. If it uses "consisting of," the presence of additional components/steps means no literal infringement. If it uses "consisting essentially of," additional components/steps are allowed only if they do not negate an element or materially affect the basic and novel properties of the invention. (Shire Dev.; Multilayer Stretch; CIAS; Norian.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct Infringement—Doctrine of Equivalents (DOE)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the accused product/method does not literally infringe an asserted claim, the jury must decide whether it infringes under the doctrine of equivalents by having components/steps equivalent to missing claim elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze each individual claim element not literally present and decide whether the accused product/method has an equivalent for that element. Showing equivalence can be by demonstrating insubstantial differences, substantially same function/way/result, or that persons of ordinary skill would have known of interchangeability at the time of alleged infringement (though known interchangeability is not required). The same accused component may satisfy more than one element, and multiple accused components may satisfy one element. (Warner-Jenkinson; Graver Tank; Brilliant Instruments; Crown Packaging; Intellectual Prop. Dev.; Sun Studs; Hughes Aircraft; In re Kelley.) Practice note: if claim is literally infringed, DOE need not be applied; DOE available only for elements not literally met.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on Doctrine of Equivalents—Prosecution History Estoppel
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patentee made representations or narrowing amendments related to patentability during prosecution, a presumption arises that equivalent subject matter was surrendered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prosecution history estoppel is determined by the court; the following instruction should be given only if the court has determined estoppel applies as a matter of law. If estoppel applies to certain elements, the doctrine of equivalents cannot be applied to those elements and they must be found literally present for infringement. (Festo; Festo (Fed. Cir.); Warner-Jenkinson.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on Doctrine of Equivalents—Subject Matter Dedicated to the Public
rubrics_metrics.description: If the court determines that certain subject matter from the patent has been dedicated to the public, the doctrine of equivalents cannot be applied to those elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This instruction is given only if the court has determined dedication to the public applies as a matter of law. Elements so dedicated must be literally present to find infringement; other elements may be assessed under DOE. (SanDisk; Pfizer v. Teva; PSC Computer Prods.; Toro; Johnson & Johnston.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Actively Inducing Patent Infringement (Inducement to Infringe)
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish that the defendant actively induced infringement, the plaintiff must prove it is more likely than not that (A) a single actor is responsible for direct infringement (all components/steps), and (B) the defendant actively induced those acts of infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To prove inducement the plaintiff must establish four elements by a preponderance: (1) the defendant aided, instructed, or otherwise acted with intent to cause acts by the alleged direct infringer that would constitute direct infringement; (2) the defendant knew of the patent or showed willful blindness to its existence; (3) the defendant knew, or showed willful blindness, that the actions of the alleged direct infringer would infringe at least one claim; and (4) the alleged direct infringer infringed at least one claim. Willful blindness requires subjective belief of high probability a patent existed and deliberate actions to avoid learning of it. (35 U.S.C. § 271(b); TecSec; Commil; Sanofi v. Watson; Limelight; Global-Tech; Takeda; Info-Hold; DSU Medical; Metabolite; Ferguson Beauregard; Hewlett-Packard.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement by Supply of All or a Substantial Portion of Components Abroad (§ 271(f)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: To show infringement under §271(f)(1), the plaintiff must prove that: (1) the product as intended to be assembled outside the U.S. included all elements of at least one asserted claim; (2) the defendant supplied (or caused to be supplied) components from the U.S. that made up all or a substantial portion of the invention of that claim; and (3) the defendant specifically intended to induce the combination of those components into a product that would infringe if assembled in the U.S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A "substantial portion of components" is a quantitative, not qualitative, assessment; the export of a single component of a multi-component invention cannot create liability under §271(f)(1). Section 271(f)(1) does not apply to method claims because §271(f) requires components be 'supplied.' (35 U.S.C. § 271(f)(1); LifeTechs v. Promega; Cardiac Pacemakers; Microsoft v. AT&T.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Contributory Infringement (§ 271(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish contributory infringement, the plaintiff must prove each of the following is more likely than not: (1) the alleged direct infringer directly infringed a claimed invention; (2) the defendant had knowledge of both the patent and the direct infringement; (3) the defendant sold, offered for sale, or imported in the U.S. a component of the infringing product or an apparatus for use in the infringing method; (4) the component or apparatus is not a staple article or commodity of commerce capable of substantial non-infringing use; (5) the component or apparatus constitutes a material part of the claimed invention; and (6) the defendant knew the component was especially made or adapted for use in an infringing product/method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A "staple article or commodity of commerce capable of substantial non-infringing use" has other substantial uses that are not occasional, farfetched, impractical, or experimental. Defendant's knowledge may be shown by willful blindness (same definition as for inducement). (35 U.S.C. § 271(c); Commil; Global-Tech; Aro Mfg.; Toshiba v. Imation.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement by Supply of Components Especially Made or Adapted for Use Abroad (§ 271(f)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: To show infringement under §271(f)(2), the plaintiff must prove: (1) the defendant actually supplied or caused components to be supplied from the U.S. into a foreign country; (2) the defendant knew or should have known that the components were especially made or adapted for use in a product that infringes a claim; (3) those components have no substantial non-infringing use; and (4) the defendant intended for the components to be combined into that product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is not necessary that the components actually be combined into an infringing product, so long as the defendant intended the components to be combined into a product that would have infringed if combined in the U.S. For §271(f)(2), a "substantial use" is one that is not occasional, farfetched, impractical, experimental, or hypothetical. (35 U.S.C. § 271(f)(2); WesternGeco; Microsoft v. AT&T; Cardiac Pacemakers; Waymark; Rotec.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement by Import/Sale/Offer for Sale/Use of Product Made by Patented Process (§ 271(g))
rubrics_metrics.description: To show infringement under §271(g), the plaintiff must prove that: (1) the defendant imported into the U.S. or, within the U.S., sold/offered for sale/used a product that was made by a process that includes all steps of at least one claim; (2) the product was made between the patent issue date and the patent expiration date (or date of trial as applicable); and (3) the defendant imported/sold/used the product between the issue date and the expiration (or date of trial).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The jury must decide whether the product was "made by" the claimed process. If the product was materially changed by later processes or is only a trivial/non-essential part of another product, it was not "made by" the claimed process. Infringement under §271(g) does not require a single entity to perform the patented process. (35 U.S.C. § 271(g); Syngenta; Amgen; NTP v. RIM; Mycogen; Biotec; Eli Lilly v. American Cyanamid.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary of Invalidity Defense (burden and standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: The defendant contends that the asserted claim(s) are invalid. The defendant must prove by clear and convincing evidence that each asserted claim is invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The jury must determine invalidity claim-by-claim; the instruction will be followed by more detailed invalidity contentions (e.g., anticipation, obviousness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior Art Defined (pre-AIA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art includes items received into evidence during trial such as: (1) any product/method publicly known or used by others in the U.S. before the claimed invention was invented; (2) any product/method that was in public use or on sale in the U.S. before the cutoff date; (3) any patents that issued before the cutoff date; (4) any publications having dates of public accessibility before the cutoff date; and (5) any product/method that was made by anyone in the U.S. before the date of invention where the claimed invention was not later abandoned, suppressed, or concealed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The instruction identifies the specific prior art items the defendant contends are prior art. Citation: 35 U.S.C. § 102 (pre-AIA).
